articles.title: Do leaders matter?
articles.content: THE age-old debate over the role of individuals in history continues. Do leaders shape history or is history the product of underlying social and economic structures? Can leaders bring about change in society and determine national outcomes? Proponents of the ‘great man theory’ have argued that history is the biography of great leaders. This has been contested by others who insist economic and social forces are decisive and impose constraints on what individuals can do. But can individuals transcend structures in moments of crisis? A provocative new book joins this debate. In Profits, Prophets, Coaches, and Kings: (When) do Leaders Make a Difference Jared Diamondexamines whether individual leadersalter the course of their societies. The study marks a break from the American author’s earlier books which earned the Pulitzer Prize winner much fame. But his bestselling 1997 book Guns, Germs, and Steel and other works also attracted criticism for geographic determinism and playing down human agency. His latest book reverses the lens. Across politics, business and sports, it examines whether individual leaders play a decisive role in shaping the world around them, and under what conditions if they do. He considers how the interplay between an exceptional individual and historical circumstances determines success or failure. At the book’s outset, Diamond narrates the incident of March 1930 when Adolf Hitler’s car was hit by a huge trailer truck in which he survived. Three years later, Hitler became chancellor of Germany and unleashed the Holocaust and World War II, in which millions of people were killed. He asks whether these horrific events would have happened if Hitler had died in the car crash. Some will argue things would have turned out differently. Others would point to the humiliation inflicted on Germany by the Treaty of Versailles, by the hyperinflation it suffered and the fact that antisemitism was deeply embedded in the country well before Hitler’s rise. That makes it hard to decide whether Hitler made a difference. This, Diamond says, exemplifies the question of whether leaders determine outcomes, for better or for worse. The role individuals play in shaping history has always been a contested issue in an age-old debate. He mentions three competing schools of thought in this debate. One sees exceptional and heroic leaders determining history. The opposite view is that leaders are constrained by circumstances and have little influence on events. An in-between view holds that individual leaders sometimes do and sometimes don’t make a difference. His book takes a middle ground in this debate. For the author, the key question is under what conditions can leaders make a difference. In his discussion of leaders’ impact on history, Diamond sets what he calls the Hamlet test. This refers to whether any contemporary person had comparable qualities to achieve a similar outcome as the individual being assessed. In Shakespeare’s case, his unique talent meant no other Elizabethan could have written Hamlet if Shakespeare hadn’t done so. He cites the example of independent Botswana’s first president as a political figure who passes the Hamlet test. Seretse Khama’s policies made his country well-governed and not consumed by civil wars or diamond revenues being wasted on ostentatious projects. Although he leveraged Botswana’s inherent advantages and his position as a tribal leader, his contributions to his country would not have happened under another founding president. No other figure had comparable skills. He was an effective leader at a particular place and time, and therefore made a difference. Leaders however gifted, Diamond says, can be effective only in certain circumstances. For example, Genghis Khan, who established the largest land empire in history, had exceptional qualities but was lucky enough to be born “at the start of the wettest decade in the last 2,000 years on the steppes of Central Asia”. In other words, a military and administrative genius was helped crucially by climatic factors which had favourable economic, social and demographic consequences. Therefore, much turns on enabling conditions. Diamond draws up a list of 22 modern leaders — familiar names — and asserts that historical figures may be forces for either good or bad. Some leaders led their countries to independence and left lasting legacies. Others established dictatorships and systems that did not outlive them. Some leaders had enough power to execute their policies and make an impact. Being at the right place and at the right time, their context aided them to make a difference. One conclusion he draws is that those who made a difference rarely left office voluntarily — the two notable exceptions being Nelson Mandela and Lee Kuan Yew. He regards education as an important variable in a leader’s effectiveness. He cites the cases of Lee Kuan Yew and South Africa’s president Thabo Mbeki, trained in economics, whose countries’ economies grew spectacularly under their leadership. His account of leaders who contributed positively — and negatively — to national economic growth is particularly insightful. In discussing business leaders, Diamond notes that many famous names notably Jeff Bezos, Bill Gates, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg are credited with changing the world. But were they uniquely qualified to accomplish what they did? He concludes that none of them pass the Hamlet test. They are important and successful risk-takers in modern business but they were all replaceable. If Bezos hadn’t built an online ‘everything store’, someone else would have, as its time had come thanks to the explosion of the internet. These business leaders made a difference but not the kind that shapes a society’s trajectory. Diamond concludes that context, timing and a leader’s abilities determine impactful leadership. Some situations offer an opportunity for leaders to make impactful decisions while other situations severely constrain a leader. “A leader’s lowest potential for impact is under circumstances making it improbable that a single person could have changed the outcome,” he writes. There is much in the book to criticise. In places, Diamond’s what-if counterfactuals confuse rather than clarify. His “natural experiment” methodology of comparing similar societies or business firms facing similar crises but led by different individuals, in order to isolate the leader’s impact, also raises questions. History rarely provides comparable cases. Although he acknowledges the importance of charisma, he says too little about the distinctive qualities that leaders need to be effective. Still, it is an engaging book that makes an important contribution to a debate that will undoubtedly continue for years to come. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: AI and social catastrophe
articles.content: OVER the past 12 months, the capabilities of frontier AI models have remained a central topic of debate. Recent performance demonstrations across a variety of technical fields (maths and bio-genetics in particular) show that scepticism around raw capability at least is a dated position. However, there are still question marks around financial viability, regulation of broad-based societal risks, and impact on workers and labour more generally. The latter two deserve more scrutiny. The first concern, around broad-based risks, has gained quite a bit of attention with a spate ofresignationsfrom top AI companies, with departing individuals claiming that AI poses a serious risk to society and carries a non-zero chance of triggering human extinction. What is the pathway of such a catastrophe? The most common position at this point is that, in the absence of clear ethical guardrails, AI tools can be used to create biological weapons of the sort that could trigger large-scale human loss. Others think that, in the wrong/rival hands, AI could be used to trigger weapons of mass destruction. These fears appear to be fairly fantastical, and the timing with which they’re being made public — just when the frontier models are poised for initial public offerings — suggests they’re part of a Silicon Valley hype cycle. However, if these claims about capabilities and the risks they could carry are even remotely true, they pose a much simpler question. If a technology is truly this capable, then what is it even doing in private hands? Historian and economic commentator, Adam Tooze, made an insightful analogy that if we take the claims of societal risk at face value, we’re essentially developing a technology that is similar to the nuclear bomb in the type of catastrophe it can pose, and that too at a much greater scale. The impact of AI on labour markets is something that many workers will face in a variety of ways in the coming years. But the key difference is that the development of the bomb took place through the Manhattan Project, which was entirely governed and steered by the state, with private enterprise playing a junior and often strictly compartmentalised role. AI, on the other hand, is being developed by private enterprise, with private investment steering its priorities, and commercial viability shaping the discourse around it. At any other point in human history, has anything posing purported risks of this nature been allowed to emerge via a process of borderline anarchic market-led competition? The logical corollary of this parallel is that anything that poses large-scale existential risk is too important to be left in private hands. Public regulation determining its development, use, sale/purchase, and evolution becomes a necessity. And that this regulation cannot emerge from the industry itself, which is subsumed under intense competition and has a vested interest in skirting around various legalities, but rather from the state. Beyond pushback against the fearmongering, there is also some scepticism around AI’s potential to generate astronomic growth in capitalist societies. In particular, Ben Moll and Alex Imas argue in a recent Substack piece that predictions of double-digit AI-driven growth, the kind floated by Dario Amodei, Leopold Aschenbrenner, and various technologists, are unlikely to materialise within the next decade or so, even though making a textbook case for it is relatively simple. Moll and Imas argue that explosive growth is easy to generate in a standard textbook growth model. If automation steadily raises the share of tasks that machines can perform, diminishing returns to capital weaken and eventually disappear once machines can do everything. The core of their position, however, argues that this outcome depends on several assumptions that are unlikely to hold in practice. Automation would need to spread across the whole economy very quickly, not just in cognitive or remote tasks but across physical, messy, and relational work that resists mechanisation. Spending patterns would need to stay proportional even as automated goods become cheap, rather than shifting towards whatever remains scarce, which is the usual pattern of structural change. But a central facet, which these authors don’t give much attention to but others have honed in on, is that in a society where the cost of production approaches zero, there would need to be enough demand to absorb all that cheap, expanded output. Where would such demand come from once automation shifts jobs and income away from workers who spend a large share of what they earn? This brings us back to perhaps the key issue of AI capability that has been drowned out by fears of biological weapons and global catastrophe. The technology’s impact on labour markets is something that many workers will face in a variety of ways in the coming years. It’s not just about a machine replacing a human, though that is the most commonly held view. It’s also about how the threat of a machine replacing humans changes working conditions and the kind of income one can expect to receive. The history of technology adoption in labour processes is often told in large sweeps of history. Technologists tend to use common examples, such as how the arrival of machines after the late 19th century unlocked rapid growth and raised prosperity or how the creation of the ATM didn’t lead to a mass exodus of banking sector jobs. The implication is that society adapts and the outcome is usually positive. What this cheerful story misses out is that adaptation processes produce winners and losers, with the latter taking years to adjust. In a world already characterised by the deskilling of labour, people rendered jobless by a machine (or the threat of a machine) won’t suddenly find alternative employment. Those two or three decades in which the labour market sorts itself out will seem minuscule in a broad sweep of history, but for those living through this period, it will be a particularly bleak eternity.
articles.author: Umair Javed

articles.title: Funding journalism
articles.content: WHEN communities are cut off by conflict, displaced by violence, or trying to survive a humanitarian crisis, reliable information becomes even more of a practical necessity. Local journalists and public interest media outlets are often the only actors capable of reaching those communities in their own languages and through trusted channels, with the information they need to make decisions, access assistance and hold power to account. Humanitarian organisations recognise this: they depend on local media to reach affected populations in ways that few other actors can replicate. And yet, these are precisely the media organisations least likely to survive without sustained, long-term external support. Committed media support networks, such as the Global Forum for Media Development and IFPIM, are working hard to convince policymakers and donors of the evidence that without a robust media and information infrastructure, there is no resilient society. Operating in fragile and conflict-affected settings means constantly navigating insecurity, mis- and disinformation, displacement, political harassment and economic precarity. Fondation Hirondelle, a media development actor with more than 30 years of experience in such contexts, knows the difficulty of creating and sustaining public-interest media despite all odds. Short-term, project-based funding — still the dominant model — does not build resilient newsrooms. It builds precarious ones. It forces editorial teams to chase grant cycles rather than serve audiences. It rewards visibility over depth, and activity over long-term impact. Independent news media need more than short-term funding. On this 2026 World News Day, we are reminded of the importance of showing what goes into journalism that matters. This is backed up by evidence and academic research such as the global call from leading economistsurging action to protect public interest media for economic prosperity and human progress. Recognising the value of independent journalism, however, also means asking what allows it to continue. If we are serious about independent journalism as a pillar of democracy and stability, we need funding frameworks that reflect that commitment. This question is particularly urgent today. International funding for media and development is under increasing pressure, while the need for reliable, independent information is growing. At the same time, major donors are making decisions that will shape their priorities for years to come. The European Union’s negotiations over its next Multiannual Financial Framework are one important example. The decisions now taking shape will define EU external action from 2028 onwards. At the heart of that framework is the Global Europe instrument, through which the EU supports democracy, human rights, resilience, development and humanitarian action in partner countries. The choices made about the ways these resources are allocated will have direct consequences for the already limited share of international assistance that supports public interest media — including in fragile and conflict-affected contexts where that support is most needed. Without explicit recognition of independent journalism as critical democratic infrastructure, and without flexible, long-term funding mechanisms to match, there is a risk of replicating the same structural failures that have left public interest media consistently underfunded. This is not simply a question of protecting media organisations. When an independent news-room disappears, communities lose more than a source of news. They lose access to verified information, a space for public debate and, often, a channel through which their concerns can reach decision-makers. This is why funding for independent media should not be treated as an optional addition to democracy, development or humanitarian programmes. Reliable information is part of the infrastructure that allows these efforts to succeed. 2026 World News Day is an opportunity to demonstrate what journalism contributes to societies around the world — particularly in places where producing reliable information is difficult, dangerous and economically fragile. Journalists and media organisations will continue to do this work because they believe in its value. But commitment alone cannot sustain independent journalism. If we want public interest media to remain present when communities need them most, they need predictable, flexible and long-term support. The writer is director-general of Fondation Hirondelle. This opinion piece was commissioned as part of World News Day, a worldwide campaign highlighting the essential role of journalism in providing facts and clarity.
articles.author: Caroline Vuillemin

articles.title: Glimpses of hope
articles.content: AT last week’s UN General Assembly (UNGA), the secretary-general focused on three existential threats to humanity: climate change, unchecked AI, and spiralling income inequality. It is clear that these threats are complex, intersecting and perceived with varying levels of concern by geopolitical heavyweights. But these threats are not intractable. The dizzying speed at which narratives shift in this social media era means we have moved quickly from catastrophising about the climate apocalypse to predicting myriad ways in which AI will ravage society and the planet. But such widespread despair never produced a good outcome. It was helpful, then, to see more nuanced positions emerging from New York Climate Week, which unfolded at the same time as the UNGA. Here too, climate and AI were at the top of the agenda, but with less zero-sum messaging. Undoubtedly, AI’s environmental impact is significant, and arguably unconscionable, given the scale of the climate crisis, and the failure to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Data centres that power AI use land, already scarce water supplies, and immense amounts of energy, still largely derived from fossil fuels. By 2030, 40 per cent of electricity used by data centres will be for AI workloads — that equates to the residential electricity needs of all of sub-Saharan Africa (1.3 billion people), according to a 2025 study by Gartner, a technology insight company. Bloomberg New Energy Finance estimates that the AI load on data centres will increase global power sector emissions by 10pc over the coming decade. This is on top of emissions associated with other computing linked to cloud storage, video-streaming and the growing use of cryptocurrencies. The AI debate is heating up just as scientists are confirming that this year marks the tipping point beyond which restricting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius higher than pre-industrial levels is unachievable. The more evident the scale of the climate crisis becomes, the more perverse it seems to double down on a technological advance that has an insatiable appetite for electricity (fossil fuels) and water. But AI is here to stay, and plans to colonise Mars are still nascent. And so at New York Climate Week, more attention was paid to mounting claims that AI can help tackle the climate crisis. Examples of this include the use of AI for more intelligent load management for renewable energy; using AI to track pollution more effectively by pulling together disparate data sources from weather stations, satellites and private monitors; and better modelling of climate change impacts for adaptation and mitigation. There was also recognition that in a US that at the federal level is rolling back on climate commitments, American Big Tech companies are playing an important role funding renewable energy projects through multimillion-dollar contracts. The climate aspect should be a core focus of AI regulation. But this more balanced AI-fights-climate change story should not enable greenwashing by Big Tech. While there are hopes that data centres will increasingly be powered by renewable sources, the overall effect of bringing coal- or gas-fuelled power plants online now to sate immediate energy needs is hugely damaging. It stymies efforts that have been underway to retire fossil fuel-based power generation. In a recent paper, Ketan Joshi, a clean energy and corporate accountability researcher, highlighted that many claims of AI’s climate impact link back to case studies being published by Big Tech and other corporates that are deeply conflicted, rather than independent academic research. Joshi’s paper also points out that the AI that can be used to benefit the climate is ‘traditional’ machine-learning which has a much lower environmental impact than consumer-generative AI tools, such as Copilot, Gemini or ChatGPT, that are more resource- With this awareness comes the pressure on AI consumers to make more ethical choices about when and how they use AI. Since generative AI has a greater environmental cost, users should be more informed about when they genuinely need the extra computational power (stick to Google for the recipes; images and video are more wasteful than text; don’t automatically opt in for the AI search option). But it’s unfair to put the onus on end users. The climate aspect should be a core focus of current AI regulation and sovereignty debates. As with political discourse in recent years, it’s important that these issues not be hijacked by zero-sum thinking, knee-jerk polarisation and absolutism. The dire warnings punctuated by glimpses of hope in New York last week are a reminder that the only way forward — on the climate, AI and much else — is on the basis of empirical evidence, nuance, transparency and accountability. The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
articles.author: Huma Yusuf

articles.title: Facts first
articles.content: WORLD News Day comes at a difficult moment for journalism. Never has so much information been available so quickly, and never has it been so easy for propaganda, lies, manipulated imagery and AI-generated material to circulate alongside fact. The challenge is no longer simply access to information, but knowing what deserves belief. This year’s message, ‘Choose trusted journalism’, is therefore particularly apt. Yet trust cannot be demanded by news organisations as a birthright. It must be earned through the daily, often invisible work of checking claims, verifying evidence, consulting multiple sources, separating fact from opinion and correcting mistakes openly. In a media environment that rewards speed, outrage and certainty, such principles may appear old-fashioned. They are, in fact, journalism’s strongest defence. They also remain essential because false information can inflame tensions and erode confidence in institutions. Newsrooms must look inward. Every sensational headline, careless error or blurring of reporting and commentary weakens public confidence and makes serious journalism harder to distinguish from the flood of material surrounding it. But responsibility does not rest with journalists alone. In Pakistan, the work of verification is made more difficult by pressures on reporters and news organisations, restricted access, interruptions to communications and the use of legal and administrative measures that inhibit independent reporting. When journalists cannot investigate freely, citizens know less about the exercise of power. When communications are blocked during moments of crisis or political tension, rumour gains ground. This is why press freedom and public access to credible information are inseparable. A society cannot demand trustworthy journalism while simultaneously making the practice of it more precarious. That is why World News Day should be less a celebration of the press than a reminder of mutual obligations. Journalists owe the public accuracy, fairness, independence and the humility to correct themselves. Governments owe journalists the freedom to ask difficult questions, pursue uncomfortable facts and publish without intimidation. Readers, too, must learn to recognise the difference between reporting built on evidence and content engineered for reaction. News organisations can help by being more transparent about how stories are sourced, verified and corrected, and by resisting pressures that reward sensationalism over substance. The problem of misinformation will not be solved by adding yet more information to an already crowded stream. What matters is whether information has been questioned, corroborated and placed in context. In an age when technology can create convincing falsehoods in seconds, scrutiny is not an optional extra. It is the value journalism must continue to provide — and the reason it must continue to be protected.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Expanding surveillance
articles.content: PUNJAB’S decision to extend its digital surveillance network should be appreciated. However, the question is what the government does with the vast amount of data it is collecting. The expansion to 98 tehsils will take the network well beyond its existing urban footprint. The present network uses systems such as automatic vehicle registration-plate recognition, facial recognition, video analytics and crime-pattern analysis. The potential benefits are considerable. Properly integrated surveillance can improve police response, help identify suspects and stolen vehicles, provide digital evidence, map crime patterns and allow scarce policing resources to be deployed effectively. It can also improve traffic management and response to women’s safety and crime reporting. But cameras alone do not make cities safer. The government appears to be expanding the hardware much faster than it is developing the institutional capacity to turn data into intelligence. This is where the project needs greater attention. Punjab is generating an enormous stream of potentially valuable data from cameras, emergency calls, traffic systems, police records and other digital platforms. However, there is little public evidence that this information is being systematically combined and analysed to understand the causes, patterns and geography of crime. The reported 70pc reduction in serious crime is encouraging, but such claims need independent verification. A fall in reported incidents in areas covered by cameras is not, by itself, proof that surveillance caused the decline. The larger opportunity lies in using the network as a public safety intelligence system rather than treating it primarily as a surveillance project. Data should be integrated with police investigation, prosecution and court outcomes. This could help explain why cases fail, where investigations break down and which policing interventions work. There is another requirement: safeguards. As surveillance expands into union councils and public spaces, rules governing access, retention, sharing and use of personal data become essential. Facial recognition and other AI tools should not become a licence for indiscriminate monitoring. Access to sensitive data must be logged and audited, with penalties for misuse. The technology can improve policing, but only if the authorities develop the analytical capacity, accountability and institutional discipline needed to extract its full value.
articles.author: Editorial
